en: *Explanation of the Repentance of the Six Sense Organs in the Mahāyāna*, composed by Wonhyo.
According to the Dharma-realm for those who have first begun their practice, there is not a single movement among the four modes of deportment that is in vain; they maintain mindfulness.

The inconceivable virtues of all Buddhas constantly contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) to dissolve and eliminate karmic obstructions for the sake of the infinite sentient beings of the six realms.
I take refuge in the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions.
These Buddhas are neither different nor are they one;
the one is all, and all is one.
Although there is nothing in which he dwells, there is nothing in which he does not dwell;
although there is nothing he does, there is nothing he does not do.
This is true for each and every mark of excellence, each and every pore.
Throughout boundless realms and to the end of the future,
they act without obstruction, without hindrance, and without distinction,
teaching and transforming sentient beings without ceasing.
Why is this so? Because throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, within a single speck of dust and a single thought-moment,
birth-and-death and nirvana are neither two nor distinct.
The Great Compassionate Prajñā neither grasps nor abandons,
because it is conjoined with the attainment of the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
Now, in this very place, the Lotus Treasury World-realm...
Vairocana Buddha sits upon a lotus pedestal,
emitting boundless light and gathering immeasurable sentient beings.
They turned the Great Vehicle Wheel of Dharma, which has nothing to turn;
the great assembly of Bodhisattvas filled the void,
receiving the Great Vehicle Dharma-joy that is without anything to be received.
Yet now we are all together in this single reality, the faultless Three Jewels;
yet we neither see nor hear, being like the deaf and the blind,
and thus lacking the Buddha-nature.
Why is this so? Because, through the inversion of ignorance, one falsely constructs external objects;
clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self," one creates various kinds of karma.
I have long believed that my own obscurations prevented me from seeing or hearing [the Dharma],
just as a hungry ghost sees fire when standing by a river;
therefore, before the Buddha, I now feel profound shame and remorse.
Having resolved to attain Bodhicitta, I sincerely repent:
from time immemorial, myself and all sentient beings have been intoxicated by ignorance and have committed immeasurable transgressions.
There is no evil among the five heinous crimes or the ten unwholesome actions that they have not committed;
whether acting themselves, inciting others, or rejoicing upon seeing others act,
such transgressions are beyond counting.
This is that which has been realized and known by all Buddhas, worthies, and sages.
For transgressions already committed, one gives rise to profound shame and remorse;
for those not yet committed, one dares not commit them again.
These various offenses truly do not exist.
It is through the combination of various conditions that they are conventionally designated as "karma.
Thus, karma does not exist within the conditions, nor does it exist apart from the conditions.
It is neither internal nor external, nor does it abide in between.
The past has already ceased;
the future is not yet born; the present does not abide.
Therefore, that which is produced is without arising because it has no abiding. If it previously existed, it would not be "arising";
if it previously did not exist, what could arise?
If one says it was originally non-existent and now exists, [this is untenable].
Regarding the statement that "the conjunction of two meanings is called arising":
when it was originally non-existent, there was no present existence;
when it is presently existent, it is not the case that it was originally non-existent.
If prior and posterior do not coincide and existence and non-existence do not conjoin,
then since these two meanings do not unite, how can there be arising?
Since the meaning of conjunction is already destroyed, disintegration likewise cannot be established.
Neither conjoined nor dispersed, neither existent nor non-existent.
When there is no time and no counterpart, how can there be non-existence?
When there is time and no non-existence, in relation to what could there be existence?
Neither priority nor posteriority, neither existence nor non-existence, can be established.
One should know that the nature of karma is fundamentally unarisen;
from the very beginning, it has never undergone birth.
Where could there be non-arising?
Neither arising nor non-arising can be apprehended;
even that which is said to be unapprehendable cannot itself be apprehended.
The nature of karma is thus, and the Buddhas are likewise.
As it is said in the sutra:
"For example, just as sentient beings perform various karmas..."
Whether wholesome or unwholesome,
it is neither internal nor external;
thus, the nature of karma is neither existent nor non-existent.
It is likewise so:
that which was originally non-existent now exists, yet it does not arise without a cause;
there is no agent and no recipient.
When the conditions of time and circumstance converge, one obtains retribution.
If a practitioner can repeatedly contemplate such true reality while performing repentance,
even the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes will be rendered powerless.
Just as empty space cannot be burned by fire,
so too those who are heedless, lacking shame and dread of blame,
and unable to contemplate the true nature of karma [are likewise unburnable].
Although there is no inherent nature to sin, one will still enter hell,
just as an illusory tiger returns to devour its creator,
the illusionist. Therefore, you should [repent] before the Buddhas of the ten directions.
One should generate deep shame and remorse and perform repentance.
While performing this repentance, do not regard it as something that has been done;
one should immediately contemplate the true nature of repentance, wherein the offenses for which one repents are fundamentally non-existent.
How could there be one who is able to repent?
Since both the act of repenting and that which is repented of are unattainable, where could there be a dharma of repentance? Having thus repented regarding all karmic obstructions—
One should also repent of the negligence of the six sense-faculties.
From beginningless time, both myself and all sentient beings have failed to understand that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.
Through false imagination and inverted views, they calculate "self" and "what belongs to self.
Internally, they establish the six sense organs as a basis from which consciousness arises;
externally, they treat the six sense objects as truly existent.
They do not realize that all these are produced by their own minds,
being like illusions or dreams, ultimately non-existent;
yet within them, they recklessly conceptualize characteristics such as male and female.
Giving rise to various afflictions, they bind themselves with their own fetters;
long submerged in the ocean of suffering, they do not seek the essential way of escape.
How truly strange it is when they practice meditative concentration!
It is just as when one is asleep, the hindrance of torpor shrouds the mind,
causing one to falsely perceive oneself being swept away by a great flood,
unaware that this is merely a creation of the dreaming mind.
That is to say, while actually drowning and experiencing great terror, before one has yet awakened, one further conceives another dream, thinking:
"What I have seen is a dream; it is not real."
Because his mental nature was sharp, he recognized within the dream that it was a dream;
thus, he felt no fear regarding his immersion in water,
yet he was still unable to realize that his body was lying upon a bed.
Moving his head and shaking his hands, he diligently sought eternal awakening.
At the moment of eternal awakening, he traced back the conditions of his previous dream;
both the water and the flowing body were found to be utterly non-existent.
One sees only that [the self] has been lying peacefully on the bed from the beginning;
long dreams are likewise so.
Ignorance shrouds the mind, causing it to falsely manifest as the six realms of existence.

Amidst the internal causes of the eight sufferings of saṃsāra, through the inconceivable permeation of all Buddhas and by relying externally upon the power of the great compassionate vows of all Buddhas,
one attains a semblance of faith and understanding.
I and all sentient beings merely sleep within a long dream, falsely calculating it to be real;
we are bound by the six sense-objects, whether agreeable or disagreeable, and by the two marks of male and female.
All of this is my dream;
it is forever devoid of substantial reality.
What is there to be anxious about or to rejoice in? What is there to be greedy for or to feel hatred toward?
Reflecting on this dream-visualization again and again,
one gradually cultivates and attains the "dream-like samādhi."
By means of this samādhi, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
One awakens suddenly from the long dream and immediately realizes that,
from the very beginning, there has never been any cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
However, one should lie down with a single-minded focus, just as on a bed.
If one can remain thus detached,
one should reflect upon this repeatedly.
Although one encounters the six sense objects, one does not regard them as real;
being burdened by afflictions and shame, one cannot indulge in self-indulgence.
This is called the Mahāyāna repentance of the six sense organs.
Mahāyāna Repentance of the Six Sense Organs (Ṣaḍ-indriya)
